title: Split rank of triangle and quadrilateral inequalities
contribution: Proves that a non-trivial facet of the two-row relaxation P(R,f) has finite split rank iff its induced lattice-free set is not a type-1 triangle, by giving explicit sequences of split disjunctions that generate each triangle and quadrilateral cut.
problem_entry: Cook-Kannan-Schrijver's T1 triangle has infinite split rank; asks which other two-row facets are reachable by repeated split cuts (p. 1).
key_idea: Constructive: alternate the (x1<=0)v(x1>=1) and (x2<=0)v(x2>=1) disjunctions and keep one valid inequality per step, which converges to the target; harder shapes (T2A, T3, Q1, Q2) take one rank more than auxiliary cuts of shapes already handled (pp. 15-16, 21, 28-37).
assumptions: f in Q^2 minus Z^2, rational R, cone(R)=R^2 after Prop. 4.1; simplifying non-split-set assumptions in the T3/Q2 proofs, not written out (pp. 2, 6, 30, 35).
proof_devices: Shape lemma, projection and lifting propositions reduce the problem to <=4 continuous variables (pp. 5, 8-11)
Unimodular/integral-translation invariance and standard T2B triangle (Obs. 5.1 p. 11; Prop. 7.2 p. 13)
Validity checked on x-vertices of support <=2 (Obs. 7.1, Prop. 7.4, p. 14)
Closed-form recursion on intersection points + monotone bounded sequence for finite convergence (Lemmas 7.5-7.6, pp. 19-20)
Two-phase divergence argument with an appendix length computation (Lemmas 7.12-7.13, pp. 25-27; p. 39)
Vertex enumeration by support size for T3 and Q2 (pp. 31, 35-37)
positioning: Extends Andersen-Louveaux-Weismantel-Wolsey and Cornuejols-Margot facet classifications; the one negative case comes from Cook-Kannan-Schrijver; recovers rank 2 for sequential-merge and two-row mixing inequalities (pp. 1, 5, 29, 31).
writing: Main theorem plus a six-step outline mapped to sections before the technical work (pp. 4-6); fixed figure legend; plainly says the authors are unable to prove convergence of one sequence in one case (p. 21).
limits_future: Finite but unquantified rank for most T2B cases (exactly 2 only in Case 3, p. 20); non-split-set subcases left to the reader (pp. 30, 35); no future-work section.

method_links.note: If-and-only-if theorem whose boundary is the known T1 counterexample; states where its own construction fails
MILP-side source of the substructure paradigm (two-row relaxation vs split closure), not yet an import into MINLP

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: reduce to a canonical instance through monotonicity lemmas
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: shape, projection and lifting lemmas plus unimodular standardization shrink the problem to <=4 columns and standard triangles before the case analysis

transferable: Prove finite rank constructively: an explicit disjunction sequence with a keep-one-inequality rule, so that validity is a finite vertex check (pp. 14-16)
Reduce many columns to <=4 by shape/projection/lifting lemmas before case work (pp. 5, 8-11)
Get hard shapes from easy ones by building auxiliary cuts of an already-handled type and adding one disjunction (pp. 28-30)
Prove finite convergence by turning a moving intersection point into a scalar recursion and showing monotonicity and the limit (pp. 19-20)

quotes.text: The proof is constructive and given a facet-defining triangle or quadrilateral inequality we present an explicit sequence of split inequalities that can be used to generate it.
Instead of considering only facet-defining inequalities, we analyze the split rank of the larger set of valid inequalities whose induced lattice-free set is described in Proposition 2.3

title: The Chvátal-Gomory closure of a strictly convex body
contribution: Proves that the Chvatal-Gomory closure of a strictly convex body, and of its intersection with a rational polyhedron, is a rational polytope, extending Schrijver's polyhedral theorem to the other end of the curvature spectrum.
problem_entry: Schrijver's polyhedrality of the CG closure had been extended beyond rational polyhedra only for rational ellipsoids; convex nonlinear IP borrows linear-IP cut ideas, so ask whether polyhedrality survives (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Every non-integral boundary point of a strictly convex body is cut by some CG cut (via Diophantine approximation); compactness then gives a finite cut set, and only finitely many further cuts can matter (Fig. 1, p. 4; Props. 3.1, 4.1, 4.2, pp. 8-10).
assumptions: Compact, full-dimensional, strictly convex C; rational polyhedron P; constraint qualification obtained from strict convexity; the proofs actually need only boundary-separation conditions S1/S2 (pp. 3-4, 9, 12).
proof_devices: Worked counterexamples to the naive integral-normal choice (Examples 2.1-2.2, 3.1, pp. 4-6)
Dirichlet simultaneous Diophantine approximation plus a fixed perturbation for properties P1/P2 (Thm 3.1, Lemma 3.2, pp. 6-7)
Continuity of the unique-maximizer map under strict convexity (Lemma 3.1, pp. 6, 14)
Open-cover / finite-subcover on the compact boundary and the sphere (Cor. 3.1, Prop. 4.1, pp. 8-10)
Large-norm cuts cannot cut interior vertices (Prop. 4.2, p. 10)
Integer Farkas + unimodular reduction for lower-dimensional sets (Prop. 5.1, p. 11)
Fenchel support-function splitting to lift face cuts (Props. 5.2-5.3, pp. 12-14)
Induction on dimension (p. 13)
positioning: Generalizes Schrijver and the authors' own ellipsoid result; explains why the polyhedral proofs (TDI, cut domination) and a polytope-sandwich approach do not extend; sits within the convex MINLP cutting-plane literature (pp. 1-2, 4).
writing: Results and a proof outline come first, small examples illustrate the obstacle, the open general case is stated with hedging, and the appendix makes the paper self-contained (pp. 2-5, 13-14).
limits_future: General convex bodies remain open and need new methods (pp. 2, 4); strict convexity is used for continuity of m_C (Remark 3.1, p. 8); no bound on the number of cuts and no algorithmic consequence.

method_links.note: Carries a MILP closure theorem into convex nonlinear IP, explicitly motivated by generalizing linear-IP ideas
Result placed at one end of the curvature spectrum with the open middle named; Remark 3.1 shows why the key separation fails for general convex bodies

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: state the theorem through the property the proof uses
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Props. 4.1-4.2 are proved under boundary-separation conditions S1/S2 and C1'/C2', which some non-strictly-convex bodies also satisfy

transferable: Finite-subcover argument: open sets of points cut by each CG cut + compact boundary give finitely many cuts (pp. 8-10)
Dirichlet approximation plus a fixed integral perturbation to manufacture separating integral normals (pp. 6-8)
Support-function (Fenchel) decomposition to lift cuts from a face F∩C to P∩C (pp. 12-13)
Rule out the obvious proof routes in the introduction and say why they fail (p. 2)

quotes.text: We observe here that while various proofs of Theorem 1.1 have been presented, unfortunately none of them seem to extend to the case of non-polyhedral convex sets.
we believe that a whole new set of methodologies and insights need to be developed to understand the structure of the CG closure of a general convex set.

title: Solving mixed integer bilinear problems using MILP formulations
contribution: Gives an exact binary-expansion MILP reformulation of integer-times-continuous bilinear programs with a polynomial-size convex hull of the single-term set, and tests it against Couenne and a McCormick-relaxation branching scheme on five instance classes.
problem_entry: Instead of strengthening spatial B&B, solve mixed integer bilinear problems as MILPs when integrality is hard; binary expansion, poor for general MILP, is exact here, and its polyhedral structure was unstudied (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Binary-expand y and linearize exactly; the hull of {z in S, x in [0,a], v=xz} is conv(S) multiplied by x and a-x (Prop. 3.1), and the superincreasing binary-expansion knapsack has explicit minimal covers, giving a polynomial-size hull (Cor. 3.5) (pp. 8-12).
assumptions: Bounded nonnegative x in [0,a], integer y in [0,b], b>=1; conv(S) a polytope for Prop. 3.1; extensions to semi-integer y and missing powers of two (pp. 3, 8, 11-12).
proof_devices: LP-strength comparison with explicit witness points and exact equality condition b=2^gamma-1 (Props. 2.1-2.3, pp. 3-6)
Hull of a union of the x=0 and x=a polyhedra via Balas disjunctive formulation and projection (Prop. 3.1, pp. 8-9)
Minimal covers of a superincreasing knapsack read from the binary digits of b (Props. 3.3-3.4, pp. 10-11)
Optimality argument for valid variable bounds (Prop. 4.1, pp. 15-16)
experiments: Five classes (MINLPLIB, bundling random+real, MIPLIB with constructed bilinear objective, integer BoxQP, disjoint bilinear); Couenne vs M-BLP vs B-BLP vs B-BLP+hull cuts in CPLEX 12.1, aligned tolerances, 1 h limit; bound and primal gaps against the best value found by any method or a 24 h Couenne run; performance profiles; mixed outcomes reported (pp. 12-22).
positioning: Contrasted with spatial-B&B strengthening (envelopes, RLT, SDP, Lagrangian, piecewise); explicitly declines to judge spatial B&B from Couenne vs CPLEX; credits referees for more instances and corrections (pp. 1-2, 12, 23).
writing: Contribution sentence ends the introduction (p. 2); per-class discussion naming where the method loses; hedged conclusion 'on certain class of problems'; dead end reported in one sentence (pp. 13, 23).
limits_future: Cuts help mostly with a bilinear objective and linear constraints; little root-gap closure on general bilinear problems; cuts not exhaustive; future work: exploit binary expansion inside problem constraints (p. 23).

method_links.note: Convexifies the single integer-continuous bilinear term jointly in an extended space rather than termwise McCormick, then tests in branch-and-cut
Each formulation inclusion comes with an exact equality condition and explicit separating points
Exact MILP and primal quality are the emphasis; bounds are reported (mu_I) but certified gap is not the deliverable

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: multiply-the-hull lemma for products with a bounded continuous variable
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: conv{z in S, x in [0,a], v=xz} is obtained from conv(S) multiplied by x and a-x via a two-piece disjunction

transferable: Prop. 3.1 recipe: union of x=0 and x=a pieces, Balas disjunctive formula, project (pp. 8-9)
Use known knapsack structure (superincreasing weights) to make an extended hull polynomial (pp. 10-11)
Reference value OPT_I = best of all methods plus a 24 h competitor run; report bound gap and primal gap separately (p. 13)
Build missing instance classes from a standard library with a stated deterministic recipe (p. 18)
When comparing formulations, give an explicit witness point for each strict inclusion and the exact equality condition (pp. 4-6)
coauthors: Akshay Gupte, Shabbir Ahmed, Myun Seok Cheon

quotes.text: Although the use of binary expansions is known to be inefficient for general MILPs [27], in our case, it gives us an exact MILP reformulation of (BLP1).

Since CPLEX is a sophisticated commercial MILP solver whereas Couenne is a relatively new open source MINLP solver, we cannot and do not wish to draw conclusions regarding the performance of the spatial branch-and-bound algorithm.

title: Covering linear programming with violations
contribution: Proves covering k-violation LPs strongly NP-hard and gives three MIP enhancements (iterative coefficient strengthening with a provable gap bound, mixing-set cuts whose projected closure is shown polyhedral, and an overlap-removing branching rule) that cut some solve times from days to hours.
problem_entry: Natural MIP for covering LPs with at most k violated constraints performs very poorly; the complexity of the covering subclass was open; CPLEX difficulty is measured first by data feature (pp. 1-2, 5-6).
key_idea: Tighten the big-M coefficients by a fixed-point of LPs over the current relaxation, adapt mixing inequalities from chance-constrained programming, and add reversed constraints as local cuts to remove branch overlap (pp. 7-8, 10-15).
assumptions: Nonnegative covering data scaled to b_i=1; analysis assumes c_j>0, a_ij>0 for simplicity; gap bounds depend on data variability rho or coefficient range (pp. 2, 8, 13).
proof_devices: Strong NP-hardness from vertex cover via an intermediate decision problem and rounding claims (Lemma 1, Thm 1, pp. 3-5)
Monotone bounded sequence for termination of coefficient strengthening (Prop. 3, pp. 7-8)
Comparison sequence by aggregating all rows into one averaged row, giving gap bound m(1-rho)/(m-rho k) (Lemma 2, Thm 4, pp. 8-10)
Equivalence of basic mixing closure and simple disjunctive closure, hence polyhedral (Prop. 8, Cor. 9, p. 13)
Gap bound by coefficient range and NP-hardness of separating over D (Prop. 10, pp. 13-14)
experiments: CPLEX 12.1 default as baseline; portfolio (n=20, m=200, k=15, with/without budget) and Tanner-Ntaimo vaccination instances up to m=2000; root gap closed, B&B time/nodes, percentage improvement, and total time including root work; negative results and per-instance ranges reported (pp. 5-6, 15-20).
positioning: Adapts Luedtke et al. mixing-set approach and Gunluk-Pochet inequalities; gives a direct strong NP-hardness proof rather than modifying the weak packing result (pp. 3, 11).
writing: Computational headline in the abstract; numbered observations hedged with 'perhaps'; mechanistic explanations of why each technique wins or loses; conclusion lists mixed outcomes (pp. 1, 6, 17-20).
limits_future: Cut management in the tree unsolved; separation complexity of the mixing closure unknown; root effort grows like m^2 and is not worth it on easy instances; better mixing separation suggested (pp. 14, 17, 19-20).

method_links.note: Problem and separation hardness proved; open separation complexity stated as unknown
Relaxation-strength bounds are data-dependent (rho, coefficient range), unlike the later data-independent ideal
No ceiling or stripped instrument; but difficulty drivers (k, density, objective) are isolated against the default solver before any method

quotes.text: To assess the practical computational difficulty of CKVLP, we next report on the performance of CPLEX, a state-of-the-art MIP solver, on randomly generated instances of the MIP (4).
we observe that significant effort on coefficient strengthening is not justifiable for instances that CPLEX can solve in under 1500 seconds.
